result:
At the back of the hardware store was a drawer labeled **Things That Probably Fit Something**.

Inside were brass washers, a wooden knob, three keys joined by a ribbon, and a small silver hinge that moved so smoothly it seemed expensive.

The owner, Mrs. Vale, refused to throw any of it away.

“Everything in there has a job,” she said. “We just haven’t met the job yet.”

People came in carrying broken objects wrapped in towels. Lamps with crooked necks. Kitchen drawers that no longer stayed shut. Once, a boy brought a music box that played six notes and then clicked.

Mrs. Vale opened it with a tiny screwdriver.

“Can you fix it?” he asked.

“Possibly.”

“Will it sound the same?”

She looked up. “Do you want it to?”

He considered this. The music box had belonged to his father, who used to wind it much too tightly and insist that the clicking was part of the tune.

“Yes,” the boy said. “Exactly the same.”

Mrs. Vale examined the mechanism, then crossed to the drawer at the back of the shop. She searched for a while, pushing aside the keys and the wooden knob.

What she needed was near the bottom.

After the repair, the music box played its six notes.

Then it clicked.

The boy listened twice before putting it back in its towel.

Mrs. Vale charged him fifty cents for the part. When he had gone, she added the broken piece to the drawer.
